text:
Why wasn't the large VRAM difference mentioned in the review? I always had a hunch this was gonna cause issues much sooner than people realized and I was right. Very happy I went with the 6800XT over a 3080. The 16GB VRAM allows the Radeon GPUs to max out textures for another couple of years, literally giving you a better looking game without tanking FPS. Ray Tracing requires extra VRAM so that's out of the equation.

Most gamers upgrade their GPU every 4-5 years or so. Taking this into account, **unless you're the kind of enthusiast who upgrades every 2 years to get top gear**, the AMD cards were and still are a MUCH better buy and in my opinion this should have been obvious for tech experts. 

Keep in mind a lot of people make their purchasing decisions based off reviews and advice from channels like LTT. I personally know a lot of 8-10GB RTX3000 owners that now wish they went with AMD's 12-16GB cards. There is a mismatch between GPU power and VRAM for Nvidia cards, which is a serious issue that AMD cards don't have.   The 4070Ti and 4080 will also choke on VRAM long before the GPUs become "slow", which is unacceptable considering their ridiculous price tags, making the 7900 cards or even a 6950XT automatically a better buy for most gamers. Some new games already require over 14GB VRAM.

This should be adressed by LTT imo. Other channels have already made videos about it. I'm just wondering why you didn't see this coming and didn't even acknowledge the VRAM difference at all in your reviews.

author: @yeagmatic

text:
The Nvidia RTX 30 series currently has Resizable BAR support, so AMDs SAM isn't really an advantage. With Nvidia'a DLSS (Deep Learning Super Sample) feature being exclusive, I would have called it there and said that Nvidia's GPUs are better, but AMD isn't falling behind here either, with FSR (FX [Effects] Super Resolution) 2.0 and 2.1 being essentially identical to DLSS.

Do note that SAM is a little bit more than Resizable BAR. It works a little bit faster. The same way that DSLL produces a slightly better image than FSR. 

If you want to compare Nvidia's RTX 30-series to AMD's RX 68-series you should compare the native performance of each GPU. Of course if you care about raytracing than Nvidia is going to be ahead for now, with better quality, better performance, many more quality of life and visual quality enhancing features. 
Using the data provided in this video, at native performance, without raytracing, AMD's 68-series appears to pull ahead by just a little. But if you care about raytracing and general quality enhancements, Nvidia's 30-series is literally a generation ahead. And in terms of prices, off the shelf, Nvidia's GPUs are cheaper, but I've seen used AMD and Nvidia GPUs being sold at the same prices.

And there's plenty of them for AMD to sell to.

The upper echelon of spenders can happily wait for 4xxx and 7xxx series cards so they can watch them get scalped and marked up again, as the overall chip shortage in the world hasn't seen significant change. text: Rewind almost a decade ago and tell me how much mileage Physx got as well? Pretty sure Havok killed that off pretty soundly. I expect either a V2 of FSR or Intel's "everyone DLSS" competitor will phase out DLSS. OR strongarm Nvidia to cave and open that up like they did with G-SYNC (Adaptive Sync). Doing it first doesn't mean you own it, or will even remain the best at it. Just like, A-Sync, realtime Physics, and AA/AO, there will be one open standard as no Dev/Publisher wants to split their base on something arbitrary like that. I expect both RayTracing and/or AI Upscaling to both go this route in the future as well. I think CUDA is the only real exception that comes to mind to that mythos.

The thing for me that wasn't mentioned in the video is that as a developer I use linux. And sure Nvidia drivers are easy to get on the most popular linux distributions. On ubuntu you just check a box when installing to get the nvidia drivers. Sadly in many linux distros places and subsystems if you will, this is not the case, countless of project and distributions have broken nvidia drivers or very hard to get working nvidia drivers.

Meanwhile while Nvidia has a barely working propriety linux driver package that you may be able to install. With AMD,  the drivers are as un-complicated as an integrated GPU. AMD works with linux to get the drivers into the linux kernel. There's no getting AMD video drivers on linux, they just are a core part of linux. Going with a heavy AMD based system on Linux you would never even have to know what a driver even is in the first place. For this opensource open nature of AMD and their success in datacentres etc, I will be buying AMD cards, I don't want to even know the drivers exist nvm trying different versions for different games, different versions still for older games etc, no, AMD, it just works. text: I think the large amount VRAM is going to prove to be an advantage in the long term. Because of cars availability and pricing in my region, the pc I just built has an RTX2060 with 6GB of VRAM (cards are incredibly expensive over here, seriously). I'm actually happy with the performance I'm getting at 1080p, but here's something I'm noticing: some games can't run at their fullest, not because of lack of performance, but because of VRAM. Call of Duty warzone, for example comfortably runs at over 90-100 fps most of the time with almost everything turned on, but there's stuff I can't turn on without reaching the VRAM limit and causing the game to crash. As games become more and more demanding, the amount of VRAM necessary to run them will also increase, even at current resolutions. Some games already push to 8GB for all of their settings maxed out, which will leave a card like the 3070, which has a lot of horsepower, already close to its limit.
author: @Fernando-ek8jp

text: I have the 1080 Ti and try to push my games as much as possible, including 4k max settings. Games like Doom 2016 and Wolfenstein 2 use almost 10 gigs of VRAM (this card has 11). Until DLSS or AMD's equivalent becomes universal, I'm still going to be using native 4k for the foreseeable future, and as games are growing richer in detail, even with the improved memory compression tech in these cards, I don't think 12 gigs on the 3080 Ti will be enough to run future games at 4k max. For that reason, outside of RTX and CUDA features, I truly believe the RX 6800XT with its 16 gigs of VRAM is the better card.

text: DLSS isn't that good. You cannot upscale low res frames by using data from a previous high res frame and motion vector information. The reason is simple: 1/3 of the time you strafe the camera fast and those frames don't have a relation, so you just have low internal res. Another 1/3 you strafe slowly and again far objects are just low res wile the main character closer to you looks ok. Just the last 1/3 of the time you standing still or moving straight and from than 1/4 is a high res frame and the rest upscaled. The correct comparison should be done vs Radeon Boost with similar settings as the DLSS level. As for RT just wait for games with FidelityFX SSSR and Denoiser, today's RT is optimized for NV.

text: This video felt like about 13 minutes and 7 seconds of Linus dunking on the 6800XT... But I do have to say this. People in the comments are really acting like ray tracing is something people super care about. Well, spoiler alert, it's not really a feature that people super care about. The frame rate boost and DLSS are the main things that gamers care about, and while ray tracing is a completely nice thing to have, you can still game at a good graphical quality without it.*. My point is, *You don't need Ray Tracing to game, and you don't even need it to game at a good graphical setting. You only need it to game if you want your games to look like the realest games in the world. And most people would be completely fine if it didn't exist for personal gaming use for a little longer. That being said, RTX is still a completely nice feature that many people use, and if you want a feature and have the money, go ahead. AMD focused on the biggest thing, the frame rate improvement, which is more than enough reason to buy a 6800XT. DLSS needs to definitely implemented, and it should be able to handle ray tracing a lot better. But just saying that NVIDIA is better because of ray tracing only is not fair*. The 6800XT showed its power in the standard gaming department, it's something that I do thing NVIDIA should be scared of. That being said, I *do think the 3000 series are the better card. But for the price that the 6000 series is available at, and for the good standard gaming FPS boost, AMD is a viable option.

author: @kurouchiha

text:
@kurouchiha  The thing about Ray Tracing and 4k is that the biggest audience who buys these cards are online gamers. Ray Tracing and 4k are fine for single player games where a stable high frame rate isn't as crucial for a good experience, but who's going to risk cutting their FPS damn near in half for ray tracing and again for 4k when playing online gaming? So in my eyes that takes a big chunk away from Nvidia's stronghold. 

Also the price of a 4k high refresh rate monitor is currently outrageous to begin with, you're talking AT MINIMUM as much as these GPUs cost. So For the majority of people 1440p 144hz or even 1080p 240hz just make so much more sense this generation, and the Radeon cards are a great choice for those specs. 

Sure you wont get as good of Ray Tracing performance as Nvidia, but playable nonetheless at those resolutions especially if you don't put the ray tracing on max settings. And keep in mind that these current ray tracing games were designed specifically optimized for RTX. So I do suspect the AMD cards will look a bit better at ray tracing once we get some AMD optimized Ray Tracing games or patches on the market. And FidelityFX is in the works which should help at least lessen the gap for anyone who cares about DLSS. But just like DLSS it remains to be seen if it will be widely adopted by developers.

I'm not saying Nvidia's going to suddenly get destroyed in sales, they will still lead the market. I'm just saying AMD still has a huge market for these cards because at the end of the day they win more often than not in traditional performance which is the most important thing. They also have a big win in power supply compatibility which is another important factor for some people. And overclocking+AIB binning looks more promising with AMD cards so far compared to Nvidia. So they're going to move a lot of units this gen.
author: @KingNekro

text:
​ @KingNekro  Don't get me wrong, I am not a fanboy of either brand, I just get whatever I feel is the better option. I just wanted to address what I believe is a bad take in your original comment. Again, I don't think online gamers are the "majority" of people buying these graphics cards. I also think your average (non-competitive) gamer would put resolution over framerate. So I think a large portion of people buying these graphics cards are actually looking for the best possible visual experience with gaming and are quite content with a 60 fps experience. You can get 60Hz 4K monitors with great response time at under $300, and even much less than that during a good sale. I think you probably play a lot of competitive games or consume a lot of media that comes from that circle, but believe me that most gamers are not that demanding of their setup because they play for fun and immersion.

But yeah, I agree that with time AMD's offering will gain value as, like you said, Nvidia brought ray tracing to market much earlier than AMD and has a significant advantage. However, you could say that the fact that AMD is behind on ray tracing, DLSS, and more of this technology means that Nvidia is a more forward-thinking company while AMD is constantly playing catch up. I am definitely going for the green brand this generation since they are the clear winners in my eyes (well... that is if I could find a card in stock lmao)
author: @kurouchiha

text:
@kurouchiha  True you can definitely make that argument, but I believe AMD has been stuck playing catch up due to mismanagement before Lisa Su took over the company. And just like with Ryzen, I do believe Big Navi is the beginning of them being back on the right track which means competition is only starting to heat up which is good for everyone. 

And although Nvidia does have the better feature set right now, if you look at the performance jumps from Vega to Navi to Big Navi compared to GTX 1000 series to RTX 2000 series to RTX 3000 series, it shows AMD is improving at a faster rate than Nvidia(while also keeping the power draw a bit lower as well with Big Navi). If AMD's new team is that talented and can have a similar type of performance jump with their next gen, it really might be difficult for Nvidia to keep up in terms of pure performance. And if AMD continues to add and improve on these features with improved ray tracing and if FidelityFX manages to at least keep up with DLSS(it wont matter to most consumers whether AMD copied them from Nvidia or not) performance might be the main difference next gen. As a tech nerd I do appreciate Nvidia's innovation though.

To be honest the biggest reason I'm happy I switched from nothing but Nvidia for ages to my AMD RX 5700(aside from the fact that AMD tends to have much better sales and price drops over time, while Nvidia often keeps their cards almost the same price the whole gen), was the software. As forward thinking as Nvidia is, I wish they were more forward thinking with their software suite. 

I couldn't stand the Geforce Experience + Nvidia control panel 2 pack. Geforce Experience is flat out malware in my eyes, it frustrated me so many times forcing me to log in to an account to update my drivers(to which I constantly forgot the password for and had to switch passwords almost every time lol), and I had software updates brick the program multiple times which was extremely frustrating to fix. And the control panel is beyond antiquated. It's tolerable, but it could be more user friendly and easy to navigate and it still looks straight out of the 90's lol.

But ever since switching I just love Adrenalin2020 so much more. Driver updates are a breeze, it's more clean and modern, easy on the eyes, streamlined and easy to navigate, and has everything you need built into one easy to navigate package including OC, fan tuning, voltage tuning, Auto OC/UV for noobs, metric tools and OSD etc. Don't even need Afterburner. And I love the AMD Link phone app as well, although I don't use it to stream my games, I love the remote desktop functionality of it and it's cool being able to view and log my metrics right on my phone while playing. I know software isn't a big deal for everyone, but after nearly a decade of Nvidia's suite giving me headaches on multiple occasions, it became a pretty big deal for me. I still don't get why they force you to log into an account just to download drivers on GFE. Surprisingly my nephew had the same hatred for Geforce Experience and switched to AMD as well with his RX 580, and he already upgraded to the RX 6800 mainly because he loved Adrenalin2020 and didn't want to go back to GFE lol.

text: Been a fan for a long time, but something's shifted in your videos You've quit focusing on substance, and have veered towards sensationalism. Linus acts as if AMD announced full RT support in launch, which they did not. text:
Frankly, anyone expecting Nvidia to be embarrassed by AMD was batshit insane.

Not 6 months ago Nvidia cracked the market by releasing cards that were more than twice as powerful as the previous gen and for half the price.

AMD also spent its last years slaying the Intel beast more and more. And you expected them to both humiliate Intel, catch up to years of delay to Nvidia, and destroy Nvidia when it has the best gen in years?

AMD managed to go from being the backwater company to catching up to Nvidia and beating them in the classic department. Winning in Raytracing in their first RT gen when Nvidia already has one behind was never going to happen. AMD deserves a pat on the back and a kiss for what they've done already, that's an excellent growth.

Also, people don't mention this enough, but AMD relies on Vulkan and DX12 to power up a good part of its RT, as I understand it. Will that make them beat Nvidia? Almost definitely not, but it means the gap will shorten.

Shorthand of this gen's war is that if you want solid, powerful, classic graphics, and Linux gameplay or have a FreeSync screen, AMD is the better choice. If you want 4K/GSync and full RT power, Nvidia is the choice. If you care for none of those points, 6800 XT vs 3080 is pretty much a tie and either card will greatly satisfy you. Great job AMD for actually managing this.

text:
Yeah, I’m really excited to see what future evolutions of RDNA are capable of. This version is already ahead in a couple of areas. They’re more power efficient (although you could easily chalk that up to the superior node and not AMD’s engineers) but the most fascinating part is the Infinity Cache. Now that AMD has revealed 3D stacked cache and the strong rumors pointing towards RDNA 3 being the first chip-let based design, that opens up so many interesting possibilities for the future!

The big cache reduces the need for ever increasing bus width and memory speed which makes the cards more power efficient and cheaper to make. The main drawback is making an already massive die even bigger but chip-lets and 3D-cache solve that problem.

text:
Is there any data on how many people are actually using DLSS and Raytracing? Cause I honestly never cared for it myself, and so far I haven't run into a single other person that used it when the topic came up? Meanwhile it seems that a lot of tech youtubers are pretty hung up on it.

For me it's similar to motion blur: it hides the fact that their hardware just isn't up to the task. Motion blur was introduced mostly for console games to hide that they couldn't render above 30 fps for the longest time; and at that framerate, it arguably looks a lot better. Now we get DLSS to play "4K" (or even "8K", lol) to hide the fact that it just cannot render high enough framerates at that resolution.

So, for me, who is not a streamer, who is not using these things, nVidia is just selling a whole bunch of glass trinkets together with what is arguably good hardware. Now AMD seems to peddle roughly equivalent hardware, but without those trinkets. Doesn't sound too bad? 🤷‍♀️

text: I have to say that quote given by AMD to you guys regarding DLSS vs native resolution is just the type of trash response that has 100% now deterred me from going with these graphic cards in my build early next year. 5900X it is for the CPU, but I'm sticking with nVidia now on the GPU front. Was really looking forward to AMD pushing the boundaries and competing with nVidia in both Ray Tracing (not now, but in the future), but especially DLSS (now). As someone who has been gaming in 4K since 2016, I can safely say that DLSS is the best feature to have hit videocards in over a decade. 100% anyone who games at 4K has it enabled if any game they play can not push 4K 60FPS or dips its 1% lows below 60FPS. It's literally night and day difference compared to playing at a lower resolution and letting the display upscale. And their comment about it being not as good as native, while is true, is also ridiculous because when it's implemented correctly it's almost not noticeable from normal viewing distance. A DLSS competitor is the type of feature they need a whole team dedicated to working on and trying to beat how nVidia is implementing it, the fact that they think this should be just an afterthought is really idiotic. The fact that they mentioned those problems with DLSS too means it's very likely their version, which they're releasing soon, is going to lack behind DLSS in terms of quality.

Why would he? sure you paid for it, but do you really need it and for what? The 6800 with 16gb for example is just overkill, its not needed at all for any games today. Also you can clearly see that the memory bandwidth is big weak point of these gpus, once they test games at 4k with high quality textures. At 4k with max settings they use maybe 10gb from those 16gb and they are already choking on 256bit memory bus that is usually used in much weaker gpus, but amd try to cheat it with the massive cache here but it doesnt save these cards always. Its really good at 1080p where you use least memory but more memory you use the worse perfomance you will get with these cards. 
Nvidia probably did some testing and figured out that maybe 1-2 games from thousands can actually use more than 10gb at 4k today. So they went with 8-10gb fast memory which is just good enough for today and this kind of performance. text:
The features of RTX Voice and Broadcast to replace the background just plain sucks in terms of quality. Yes I saw nearly all reviews of major and smaller tech tubers. RTX Voice changes the voice to a degree, that is plain garbage if you want to use it to create video content. My 130$ headset with environment noise cancelling does roughly the same, without AI. The edges of the video feed when removing the background via Broadcast is green-ish, definitely not sharp and if you want quality, you just put a cheap 40$ mobile green screen behind you.
These features also come with a cost of roughly 20-25% of performance which hurts your fps. In terms of working from home, okay, the quality is good enough, but definitely not for content creation.
DLSS with the new version is okay in terms of quality and raytracing is also better objectively, no doubt about it. But 8GB/10GB VRAM on Nvidia is not enough.

I am not a fanboy, although it is great to see AMD with such a good product in terms of plain rasterization performance and I appreciate that totally. Otherwise you would have to pay the same prices for Ampere, that you did for Turing.

text:
He is nvidia biased. He did mention all the pro/cons, but did not test the pros of AMD. Here is better review:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZtxrrrkkTjc
Lots of games tested, and if you look at 1440p Ultra AMD 6800XT is ahead of 3080 with about 1-2% and even 5-6% with SAM enabled. There are some points as the AMD card got ahead in newer games such as AC Valhalla with 40% and Dirt 5 with 15%. Newer games will favor AMD because of 16GB Vram and consoles having implemented AMD gpus.
DLSS is lower then native resolution when comes to motion. Its at most same as native resolution in image quality. 
Ray tracing is the only advantage nvidia has, but still its implemented in just a few games. PS, if you look at Dirt 5 ray tracing AMD gets the fps nvidia has without ray tracing. So there are flavors. 

Imho as a conclusion 6800XT is better card if you care about: free sync, 1080p and 1440p, lower consumption, better overclocking, extra 3-4% fps from SAM, 16GB VRAM, better optimized games in the future- especially console ports
3080 is a better card if you care about: gsync, better ray tracing, 4K

text:
@MillerIndustriesInc  I'm sorry here bud, but you're just wrong here.  First, let me clear some things so no one throws the fanboy thing around: I started PC gaming just last November (almost exactly a year since I built my first rig on Black Friday), and my first CPU was a 2600x and GPU was a RX 580.  About 6 months later, I upgraded to a R5 3600 and Nitro+ RX 5700XT.  So, if anything, people can call me an AMD fanboy, and to be honest, I really was hoping AMD would pull a rabbit out of their ass and win this GPU cycle, as I really love my Nitro card. 

But your argument is mostly wrong.  If people are playing at 1080, they'd be much better going with a 3070, if not just sticking with whatever card they have/going with a last gen card, because that's more than enough power, it's cheaper than a 6800 (and even more than the XT), and you get all the features Linus mentions, which to be honest, aren't insignificant at all.  Even at 1440, I'd argue that's the card to choose (that's what I play at, and unless the stock issues continue until well into next year, that's what I'll be picking). 

Now, if I thought the 3070 wasn't going to cut it for my needs, or had the money to step up to the next tier, I MIGHT consider the XT over the 3080, but ONLY if I didn't care about RT, DLSS, and the host of other features Nvidia offers.  

Overall, I don't think this was a failure.  I think the 6800XT is a great card that can hopefully be even better once a few updates occur, and AMD shocked many even being able to compete.  And I'd agree that most people should choose the 6900XT over the 3090, if for some reason people are willing to spend that big of a price difference over the slight improvement in performance compared to the next tier (spoiler: I don't know why anyone would, but I know they will be and most the people who don't care about the money already heavily favor Nvidia products).  I also personally don't care all that much about RT, but it is the next big thing, and a lot of people will.  And MY biggest let down is that the 6800 just doesn't appear to be as good of a value as the 3070, which is even more shocking since AMD tends to be better at budget cards imo.  I think they should have cut the VRAM and released a card that at least matched MSRP, if not beat it at $449.  And down the road, they may release that card.  But unless they do it soon, it looks like my money will be going to Nvidia, assuming they ever have the stock to take it.  And your last suggestion, the one that Nvidia is screwed (or whatever you said) is so absurd, it's the entire reason I decided to reply to you.  Even with AMD closing ground overall, Nvidia is far from screwed.  Anyone who even hints at this type of reaction shows immediately how big a fanboy they are.

text:
@raawesome3851  
Man have you been brainwashed, it's not consistently better and still produces artefacts and edge halo's. While it's good as an upscaler, it's a game specific proprietary feature and not an open source one. I'd be hazarding a guess that given Super Resolution is a DXR feature of the open source Fidelity FX suite, any game using that will be cross platform and hardware agnostic, which means that it'll more likely become the DXR and Vulkan standard.
author: @magottyk

text: @magottyk  that's fair. But it is better, and is able to be used to upscale a 240p image to 720p quality. AMD just can't compete with that, at least with AI. I'll see how good their super resolution is, however. I also really need an rtx voice competitor.
author: @raawesome3851

text:
@raawesome3851  
Who wants 240p upscaled.
While it's not great that there isn't any Super Resolution at launch for comparisons, we don't actually need it for a number of reasons.
Most people run a potato version of a PC spec and not a highly tuned optimised hardware version and will usually run games toned down from maximum IQ settings to hit their target frame rate. We already saw DLSS 1.0 vs 1800p upscaling come out about even and that was before RIS (driver) and fidelity fX CAS (in game) were part of the equation.
DLSS 2.0 adds sharpening and uses a generic AI algorithm rather than a game specific one and is an improvement, but it's not as if AMD doesn't have access to AI enhancements to generate their driver generic AI algorithm and contrary to popular opinion, you don't need tensor cores for AI upsampling technology.

If you find RTX voice useful, then by all means make a purchasing decision on your needs but it isn't as if there's no alternative at all because AMD haven't specifically done one and that green screens are no longer viable because Nvidia can do it kinda without one.

I don't see how this review is bad or how he dropped the ball.  He showed the testing and gave both cards a fair shake.   the fact of the matter is Nvidia with DLSS is just better.  Raytracing is better on Nvidia.  You might not care about either of those but they are features that consumers will look to when buying their next card.  the 6800xt is 50 dollars cheaper than the 3080 but doesn't significantly outperform it.  

Last gen with the 5700xt that was a 400 dollar card that could offer you amazing gaming performance.  It was a tantalizing offer for people who didn't really care about raytracing but still wanted good gaming performance.  Now we have the 6800xt only 50 dollars cheaper but has significantly worse software over nvidia (especially for streamers) and its raytracing is just not good.  

Its just a fact.  You might as well spend the extra 50 bucks and get the 3080.  That's not me saying this generation of radeon cards are bad either.  They caught up.  I'm happy they caught up.  With the 6800xt being such a close competitor to the 3080 this is going to push nvidia to work harder or become like Intel next generation.  Linus wasn't shitting on the cards by any means.  He was pointing out their shortcomings while also showing that they are pretty close to, if not beating the 3080 in some aspects.  Its just not a recommended buy right now.  Once AMD releases their answer to DLSS it will more than likely be a more attractive offer.  Hell I'd be very interested in what the next generation of AMD cards will be like, once they get 2nd generation ray tracing.  I have a feeling that the next cycle of cards is going to be insane.

AMD showed they can compete in graphics cards as well.  This will be interesting.

text: @LithKast  I don't understand the streamer thing as with so many cores on modern cpus you can accomplish pretty much anything with the cpu. Like I have worked in hardware for a long time and the things you can do now are really crazy. Like for those of us who really know how to tinker its pretty crazy. I know nvidia has nvenc but I have not seen that actually look better than cpu streaming though its getting close. From early reports it looks like if you did want to use the 6800xt to stream its got fantastic raw framerate power but currently is behind nvenc in actual visual quality. So its fast in frames. Fluidity i feel is more important in streaming from a viewer standpoint than beauty as everything is compressed by the hosts aka youtube,twitch, etc etc and you only have limited bandwidth alloted to you so it honestly pointless to be wasting that on graphics that are going to get compressed. Thats just my opinion. I know from tinkering with 5700xt that you can stream 6 streams with almost no framerate loss from a single gpu. Thats is amazing even if it doesn't look the best. But to be honest it looks as good as nvidia did a few years ago so I don't really understand the ideas that they are terrible for stream. Is it just that its easier to use Nvida? I am genuinely asking like is it a convenience thing? Like maybe im out of touch as I am one of those people who enjoys the nitty griity of adjusting and playing with hardware so to me its part of the experience but I guess I am mostly not the normal consumer. As for his review I am speaking to its quality VS his peers in the space. He didn't even bring up the fact that that it has h.264 and          h.265 encoding and vp9, h.264, h.265, and av1 decoding. Also the whole raytracing thing is way more nuanced like actually explaining that for now AMD is behind in full scene methods of ray tracing like path tracing which is what is used in Mincraft BUT in the raytracing effects that are hybrid rendering like shadows it actually does perform well and can be comparable to nvidia in titles that use that version of raytracing. Non dlss of course. Go check out gamers nexus 6800 review to see what im talking about. I think sharing that nuance is important as many current rtx titles of which their are not many to begin with do not use the many different ray tracing effects that minecraft and control do so its good to understand what raytracing effects its struggling with and which ones its not. I have been messing with hardware for years and what amd is actually bringing in such a short amount of time is crazy the power and efficiency is better on these than nvidia full stop. Like years ago I would of told you stuff like this is impossible outside of 600watt consumption. Also I gurrentee these will get better in the next 6 months as the smooth out drivers and add features. AMD always age better than nvidia against their launch day performance metrics I have seen this over and over again. Nvidia might get 5 to 10 percent better with mature drivers over a year or 2 but honestly they woukd rather you buy the new thing every year. In contrast I have seen crazy shit on AMD like 20 percent or more improvement over a year on some of their cards. The rx 480/580 is a great example of the fine wine stuff. When it launched it was generally reviewed to be worse overall than the 1060, look at it 2 years later and it beats the 1060 sometimes by a pretty decent amount in many of the titles it lost in before. Yet people withh still pay 160 bucks for a 1060 in the used market where you can grab the AMD for half that. Maybe it wont be like that this time but I bet your going to see something like that. And I do agree with you overall what advancement we've seen this year from both companies is nuts I haven't seen anything like this in cpu or gpu in probably 10 years.

text:
I mean who cares about noise removal in chat, like its a decent option if you have crap mic or you live near an airfield, but literally 99.9% of people don't need one and don't use one even if they need it. Ray tracing as every other tech journalist has pointed out is worthless, MAYBE slightly better shadows for 50% reduction in performance isn't worth it. 

DLSS as we've seen in all of the new games is just lower quality settings, you can literally drop all settings to medium on AMD hardware and compare it to Nvidia DLSS, its essentially what it is. 

I think the RX 6800XT is the superior product for 1440p and especially all of the new and upcoming games, at 4k the 6800xt loses some of its power, I suspect its that 256bit bus that is the issue and the infinity cache at 128mb is just not enough to speed up the bandwidth enough at 4k. Even so at 4k the 6800xt is about 6% slower, but costs $50 less and at 1440p its about 2-3% faster, but again a lot of it comes down to games, certain games favor Nvidia a lot, while other favor AMD a lot. 

The RX 6800 is a tougher choice, as that $80 price premium is a bit too much, even though its about 10% faster than the RTX 3070 at 1440p. It has 16GB of vram though, so more future proof, but yeah, between the 3070 and 6800 its a tossup. If you want to save a bit of money go for the 3070, at $500 its a solid option, if you want something a bit faster with more future proofing, without breaking spending $650 or $700 then get the RX 6800.

text:
Google just took a quantum leap in computer science. Using the company's state-of-the-art quantum computer, called Sycamore, Google has claimed "quantum supremacy" over the most powerful supercomputers in the world by solving a problem considered virtually impossible for normal machines.

The quantum computer completed the complex computation in 200 seconds. That same calculation would take even the most powerful supercomputers approximately 10,000 years to finish, the team of researchers, led by John Martinis, an experimental physicist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, wrote in their study published Wednesday (Oct. 23) in the journal Nature. 

"It is likely that the classical simulation time, currently estimated at 10,000 years, will be reduced by improved classical hardware and algorithms," Brooks Foxen, a graduate student researcher in Martinis' lab, said in a statement. "But since we are currently 1.5 trillion times faster, we feel comfortable laying claim to this achievement," he added, referring to the supremacy of quantum computers.

Related: 18 Times Quantum Physics Blew Our Minds

Quantum computers take advantage of the whacky physics of quantum mechanics to solve problems that would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, for classical, semiconductor-based computers to solve.

The calculation that Google chose to conquer is the quantum equivalent of generating a very long list of random numbers and checking their values a million times over. The result is a solution not particularly useful outside of the world of quantum mechanics, but it has big implications for the processing power of a device.

Strength in uncertainty

Ordinary computers perform calculations using "bits" of information, which, like on-and-off switches, can exist in only two states: either 1 or 0. Quantum computers use quantum bits, or "qubits," which can exist as both 1 and 0 simultaneously. This bizarre consequence of quantum mechanics is called a superposition state and is the key to the quantum computer's advantage over classical computers.

For example, a pair of bits can store just one of four possible combinations of states (00, 01, 10 or 11) at any given time. A pair of qubits can store all four combinations simultaneously, because each qubit represents both values (0 and 1) at the same time. If you add more qubits, your computer's power grows exponentially. Three qubits store eight combinations, four qubits store 16, and so on. Google's new computer with 53 qubits can store 253values, or more than 10,000,000,000,000,000 (10 quadrillion) combinations. This number gets even more impressive when another fundamental and equally bizarre property of quantum mechanics enters the show: entangled states.

Related: The 11 Most Beautiful Mathematical Equations

In a phenomenon described by Albert Einstein as "spooky action at a distance," particles that have interacted at some point in time can become entangled. This means that measuring the state of one particle allows you to simultaneously know the state of the other, regardless of the distance between the particles. If the qubits of a quantum computer are entangled, they can all be measured simultaneously.

Google's quantum computer consists of microscopic circuits of superconducting metal that entangle 53 qubits in a complex superposition state. The entangled qubits generate a random number between zero and 253, but due to quantum interference, some random numbers show up more than others. When the computer measures these random numbers millions of times, a pattern arises from their uneven distribution. 

"For classical computers, it is much more difficult to compute the outcome of these operations, because it requires computing the probability of being in any one of the 253 possible states, where the 53 comes from the number of qubits — the exponential scaling [of states] is why people are interested in quantum computing to begin with," Foxen said.

Taking advantage of the strange properties of quantum entanglement and superposition, Martinis' lab produced this distribution pattern using the Sycamore chip in 200 seconds.

On paper, it's easy to show why a quantum computer could outperform traditional computers. Demonstrating the task in the real world is another story. Whereas classical computers can stack millions of operating bits in their processors, quantum computers struggle to scale the number of qubits they can operate with. Entangled qubits become untangled after short periods and are susceptible to noise and errors. 

Although this Google achievement is certainly a feat in the world of quantum computing, the field is still in its infancy and practical quantum computers remain far on the horizon, the researchers said.

text:
For those who are meme-ing the "AMD did (not) disappoint me", let's properly look at what this actually means.  And realistically what the future will unfold.
Is the 3080 the better GPU?  Yes, obviously.
Well, if that's obvious, then why should we even care about AMD's 6800/XT?  Probably because how close AMD is to NVIDIA in price to performance.  This isn't just about putting out a better GPU, but a message that NVIDIA can not do what INTEL did and just rest on their laurels.  If NVIDA wants to keep their crown, they'll actually have to fight for it.  Yes, NVIDIA is ahead due to their RTX software, but AMD catching up to that isn't unrealistic.
Furthermore, when we'll get the chance to compare the partner cards of AMD and NVIDIA, that's where we'll see the biggest competition.  And that's because NVIDIA's Founder Edition cards of the 3070/80 is unlike anything we've seen; to the point that it is arguable that it is one of the best version of those cards.  NVIDIA's partner cards are basically huge ass bricks in comparison.  And the NVIDIA FE cards have very little room for enthusiast customization.  Meaning you can't easily slap on a better cooler on the FE cards.  Whereas with the AMD GPUs, you can easily slap on a water block on them.  Cooling is much easier.  Customization is much easier.
Then we have to look at realistic future pricing.  Who here actually believes that NVIDIA will be able to maintain these prices?  We've already heard from NVIDIA partners that pricing for these specs are difficult to maintain.  There is a reason why the rumored TI/Super variants with more VRAM won't have GDDR6X but GDDR6: the costs.  As such, unlike NVIDIA, AMD started with 16gb of VRAM.  They really don't need to cannibalize their own sells with another refresh.  NVIDA has to respond with TI/Super variants with higher VRAM capacity.  NVIDIA must eat into their own sells, and cause their initial buyers to have buyer's remorse.  AMD doesn't have to worry about that, they put out a solid GPU that makes sense at the price they're asking for, could be better, but not the worse because they have wiggle room.  NVIDIA has no wiggle room.  NVIDIA should've just started with a 16gb VRAM GPU, but they did a mistake by leaving it to AMD to set the pace.  Instead of starting out strong, NVIDIA gave AMD a chance to respond.
As such, all this means is just more competition.  Never a bad thing.
In conclusion, NVIDIA is sporting the better GPU.  But the truth of the matter is, if NVIDIA was truly confident in the 3080, we wouldn't have heard of a TI/Super variant with more VRAM.

AMD are gonna prioritise 6900/6800 production, Zen3 and Xbox/PS5 production over 6700 production, and we're not likely to see large volumes of mid range/low end cards until thirst for Ryzen 5000/Xbox/PS5/6800/6900 dries up a bit.  :(

Add to that demand for new PC's being at an all time high because of lockdowns...

We probably won't see a Ryzen 5300X for a whiiiiile for the same reason.

text:
In any other situation I would be inclined to agree, but it's not applicable.  
Let's analyze the quote:

1. The subject of the despise is not "that which is beyond their reach".  So the subject is "a GPU", which is not the despised part.
2. The subject of the despise, in this case, is AMD. Not because they're "out of reach", but rather because they put something we want out of reach.
AMD promised us better availability than the 3080 release, which turned out to be a blatant lie they willingly told us, despite knowing the contrary to be true.
3. "Pretend to despise" is not even close to accurate.  This is most definitely not a case of "pretending", but rather a case of "full-blown despise".

So your quote should be more in the tune of: "There are many who most definitely despise those that put that, which was said to be within reach, far beyond reach".
Doesn't roll that easily off the tongue, but it's more to the point.

The quote can thus be translated to:
"AMD is despised by many for their blatant lies, misleading information, and broken promises.  So after all they're not that much different from Nvidia".



And here's another quote from me to you:
"Many people have too much time for trolling, due to being confound to ones house.  Purely due to 'rona and the lack of a decent GPU." :P

text:
Amd raytracing implementation is newer and better. Nvidia cores have very limited types of things they can calculate while amd cores have quite a lot in comparison. It makes perfect sense to add the ability to ray accelerate every single one of them instead of adding a special edition cores for RT specificaly. The problem is the games do not know how to use it efficiently. They were build with broken nvidia design where they could use up both rt cores and cuda cores to their heart extent, with the result being the bottleneck of one or the other. With AMD design, the game does not efficiently split the RT and vertex tasks depending on load, it tries to max out both at the same time. 
In my opinion, upsampling tricks are just that. Tricks. Cheating. Its the same thing Nvidia did ages ago to run games at lower quality and boast about huge performance.

Yeah like you would ever use any of that auto pan camera feature ever. Like streamers would ever bloody want to have their face seen when they lurk under the table. . .

text: The issue for me is DLSS. It actually is the best thing since G/Free Sync. Like, you could have the most powerful PC ever and still have screen tearing, framedrops, or nasty input lag with Vsync Now, with titles getting more and more complex, DLSS is a huge redeemer for expensive cards. Buying a card that manages DLSS is possibly more important that buying a newer card, as any DLSS capable RTX card will still absolutely crush games at 60fps and look friggin good doing it. Especially games like Cyberpunk, etc. which are bound to be performance heavy. You straight up don't have to worry because the AI overlords are on your side. I like the idea of just having a beefy boi AMD card that doesn't care about puny AI, but the fact of the matter is that as the gaming/content production industry gets larger, more time and money will be put into training DLSS, and these supersampling technologies are going to be the deciding factor in triple A game performance, VFX rendering, and more

text:
​ @sanitoeterscc3416  No, Wine (which stands for "Wine Is Not an Emulator") is a re-implementation of various Windows APIs and kernel interfaces, so in the same way that running a Direct3D 9 game in Windows 10 doesn't mean you're emulating Windows 98, using Wine doesn't mean you're emulating Windows in any way; it's API support, not emulation.
As for how common or easy it is, it's built in to Steam with their Steam Play / Proton functionality, so there it's literally just the same as installing and playing a native Linux game: click install, click play, done.
As for running Wine on its own, the most popular game launcher on Linux, Lutris, has built-in support for Wine as well as its own install scripts, which again means one-click installation and running.
You might want to actually give Linux a try one of these days; we've come a long way in the last couple of years in regards to out-of-the-box support for Windows games ;) (plus, there are still plenty of native games for Linux as well)

text:
@raawesome3851  You're correct, they work differently, but the end result of increasing the fidelity of a downsampled game is similar. Techspot did a great write-up on it. RIS isn't as powerful as DLSS, but a game rendered at ~75% with RIS on looks pretty much the same as native and comes with basically zero performance hit.

Nvidia does also have a sharpening filter, but it comes with reduced performance and looks significantly worse than RIS...even ReShade is better IMO.

text: "...but, these are up to the developer to include" - isn't this really frequently the issue with AMD stuff?  I've run into this many times over in the history of AMD vs Intel and AMD vs Nvidia - they tend to introduce powerful features that most games/software don't actually support initially.  Later on as software developers start taking advantage of said new features, performance and experience improves greatly, but it can take a long time.  Out of the box, Intel + Nvidia is the safer, more performant choice nearly every time.  Over time, that might change as developers take advantage of AMD's features, but there's no guarantee how long that will be, if ever.  I'm not necessarily an Intel or Nvidia fanboy or anything, I've definitely gone with AMD many times over the last 25 years, but more often than not, I've been happier with my Intel + Nvidia purchases over my AMD purchases time and again.

text: Wow.  This review was all over the place.  It looked rushed and poorly scripted.  The charts were difficult to understand and I could not follow what message you were trying to convey.  You talked just a little about games, showing 5 games 3 of which happen to have RT and DLSS.  I get that there is a real difference between RTX and AMD's version, and that DLSS exists and AMD does not have anything comparable.  I don't think that AMD has the scale of developers  to create proprietary software then force developers to use it - that would be like asking some small YouTube channel to compete with LTT in reviewing $50-100 thousand dollar hardware.  Nvidia have maybe 10X or 100X the number of software developers compared to AMD.  AMD is a hardware company.  Nvidia is a software company (their hardware business is only a side effect of their software business - as you alluded to when you mentioned CUDA).  For better or worse there is a real difference there, and as long as companies keep adopting Nvidia's proprietary software, the industry will become less and less competitive.  AMD made it clear that they were separating graphics from compute with the 6000 series - I think that is apparent here.   But you seem to just be telling AMD to be more like Nvidia - which would actually kill the games industry completely if that happened.  You had the opportunity to review these cards in their best light - as you normally do for most hardware in my opinion - but instead you chose to compare AMD only where they are lacking against Nvidia. The most constructive thing that you said about AMD was that Nvidia will be copying their SAM feature (which you made clear was nothing but an implementation of a PCI-E feature, and was only useful sometimes,) as soon as possible, and that people will buy the 6000 series cards because they cannot buy Nvidia cards.  Honestly you should sit back and have a rethink of the train wreck that I just sat thought twice because I thought that I must have missed some important content, like how these cards compete for normal rasterized performance across a broad set of games.

Dlss is just a pile of poo, as all upscaling is - i want the best image clarity i can possibly get with my monitor, so why would i want to reduce it by using upscaling? If it is cause people are short on gpu power, then they should have bought a lower res monitor to match their gpu in the first place, or get a better gpu. Native res or downsampling - anything else is fail. In other words all that matters to me is gaming performance - nothing more nothing less.

text: Thing I'm seeing in the graphs. The analogous performance increase at this point is SAM and DLSS (not the same tech, but it's their "punchy" technology this year). Without it 3080 stills generally beats 3800xt, and with both enabled 3080 still trounces AMD.... Especially so for the 3070 to 6800 (especially considering 6800 is a more expensive card). I don't think AMD's DLSS is going to catch up to NVIDIA considering their focus on AI over the last several years. And looking into the future pretty sure 3080 will still reign supreme over the 6800xt when it introduces SAM. Also with Raytracing becoming more prevalent the fact that Nvidia still reigns supreme there, gives even less credence to AMD.... Honestly the only thing to save AMD this year, especially marketing their 6800 more expensively than the 3070 is if they can have a higher stock, which shocker they're already out of stock. This year's graphics war is again squarely Nvidia's, I mean ffs 6800 is more expensive than the 3070, yet still gets trounced, come on AMD. Hopefully though their closer performance means in the next few years we might see their intel leapfrog occur on the GPU side (no fingers crossed for that one). The only savor for AMD might be those who want to do VR, which may want higher VRAM availability since all cards include 16gb but that's the one silver lining.

text:
Honestly, I think the Blender benchmark using ray-accelerated Radeon ProRender was just misconfigured. The amount of noise looks like adaptive sampling may have been enabled, but without using the AMD’s AI denoiser it was designed for. (It can of course also be a bug, that wouldn‘t be the first time...)
To be clear, I‘m not a fanboy. I‘ve used Radeon ProRender for one project only, there are numerous serious issues with it that turned it into a nightmare, and I definitely wouldn‘t recommend it.
That being said, without ray acceleration at least, performance was one of the few strong points for this engine for me, but that‘s from comparing 10-series and Vega cards.
I‘d also like to know if in general, LTT is running their Blender benchmarks at their default settings, or is optimising them for the specific hardware they‘re using. That can make a big difference!
I‘ve been using Blender for several years now, and in my experience CUDA performs a lot better with most settings, including the defaults, but there‘s a lot more to be gained from optimisation when using OpenCL. I can consistently lower OpenCL render times by around 30% by optimising these settings, while it‘s „only“ about 10% with CUDA.

text:
It's really all software optimisations that need to be done to make those FPS numbers the , the game has had zero time to adapt to using the libraries, and that one was specifically designed for NVIDIA which means the GPU related code is baaad for the AMD card, in a few weeks support will improve for this part of the performance of ray tracing.

A new GPU means a entirely new instruction set which is entirely different, so once they get to the optimisation step for many different games things will level out most likely.

I work in the game industry and GPU optimisation is necessary and time for software to update their engines is also required. Drawing up conclusions of a product vs another when the software was only ever written for the previous gen and mostly NVIDIA is unfair comparison to draw, because its not really an entire new arch its like the second gen ryzen CPU's right now, but I expect to see 15-20 percent more performance in the coming weeks out of those cards on certain benchmarks, there could just be bugs which they need to fix, I expect the inconsistent render times for longer vs shorter scenes is actually a bug, because throughput on GPUs optimised is generally linear for the workload.

text:
@untag4066  completely true. But here's the thing, newer consoles are advertising ray tracing as a selling point, and they're running amd hardware.
This means that future games are gonna have more and more ray tracing support which will only look better.
As for your point about 144hz displays,
You really don't need a 500+ dollar gpu for 1080p 144 hz, an rtx 2070 super /5700xt fair pretty well. Esport titles like r6s, csgo, valorant, are all playable at 400-500 fps on these gpu's at competitive settings, settings which most esport professionals use. 
As for AAA titles, the 3070 easily gets 120+ frames at ultra settings on many of them. 
As for 1440p 144 hz, the 3070 is a damn good value over the 6800 non xt, condering its 80 bucks cheaper,performs great all while having dlss and better ray tracing.
Lastly, for 4k 144 hz , the 6800xt and rtx 3080 perform nearly the same, with the 3080 edging out in some titles and the 6800xt in others. Then it comes down to whether you're fine with paying 50 dollars less but also being left without dlss and faster ray tracing.

@DoubleDragon5180  I game on a 4k Sony TV that I think cost about $1000 back in the day.  It does 4k 60hz, which really sucks when frames start lagging (a new display wouldn't fix that - my gtx 1080 can only grind so hard).  Good luck trying to get 4k 120hz working smoothly on any TV hooked up to HDMI, but whatever.   Not only that, you're going to get color degradation, trying to pump that much bandwidth to even the most modern of HDMI connections.  

My TV is getting long in the tooth, and I'm REALLY eyeing that 48" OLED CX right now, but if you really want to go with a CX, you'll be unloading $1400, and risk burn-in within a few years, if you're not super careful.  

If I'm going to be shelling out $700+ for a graphics card alone, I should probably be considering what gear I'm going to pair with that visually.  Come to think of it, if I'm going to be shelling out $700 for a graphics card, I need to think of whether my aging 7700k CPU is going to be a bottleneck.

It's going to be expensive no matter which way you dice it, so if you're broke is a joke, or squeamish about high prices, this definitely isn't the right hobby....

text:
I am a little disappointed, I suspect Linus was too, the title was probably an effort not to trigger the AMD fanboys (and click bait). I have watched a few reviews and I have gone from initial excitement to disappointment. Did you see the Portal issues on Jayz's channel? That added to the defects in rendering on 3D productivity and it looks like AMD still haven't managed to get the software right. I am also on 3840x1600 and didn't expect the performance to tail off so heavily at higher resolutions.

Still it will probably suit a lot of people at or below 1440p who aren't bothered about ray tracing, streaming, or productivity. Other reviewers clearly show AMD ahead in 1440p gaming (using rasterization). Just doesn't feel very future proof with high refresh 4K monitors dropping in price rapidly. Also those Nvidia features look niche now, as does ray tracing, but in a years time? I think AMD will have to drop the price a little, that is a lot of features added and issues avoided for an extra $50-70 (~10%). I agree that it seems hard to recommend.

Close but still unfortunately feels like an AMD Radeon release... slightly underwhelming. Next time maybe, but we always seem to be saying that?

text:
I very much appreciate how AMD helps develop and support technologies that are open. Sadly, many of them aren't as good and/or as well supported as Nvidia's proprietary tech. In the specific case of OpenCL versus CUDA for example, OpenCL support is spotty at best these days. We can Apple in part for this, who initially pushed OpenCL but later seemed to completely forget about it, even when AMD became their sole Mac GPU provider. They never seemed to they actively worked together to improve technologies like OpenCL. Or at least not in a very publicly visible way. A real shame really, since both could have greatly benefited from such a collaboration, as well as making the market for productivity-oriented GPUs more competitive. Instead Apple is transitioning to their own GPU tech, which is only going to benefit them and not the GPU world as a whole.

Anyway, what I'm saying is that I'm still patiently waiting for my RTX 3070, because CUDA is just so well supported in the machine learning field.

Finally: When benchmarking a GPU for productivity, why not also include a machine learning benchmark? This type of work is becoming more and more relevant.

text:
(Please don't get me wrong: SAM is an awesome feature, even if it's just a new marketing term for something that was already specified. Still: AMD pushed this and caused nVidia to get moving. Awesome! Also, the 6800XT is a pretty great GPU)
First off: According to Hardware Unboxed the 6800XT is on par with the 3090 at 1080p ... and even he acknowledges he's CPU bound at that resolution in many cases. So, unless you're really buying a high end GPU for 1080p gaming so you can run into a CPU bottleneck... meh?

On top of that, I find Hardware Unboxed kinda hard to take seriously. 
For the 6800XT review, he doesn't even so much as blink when the 6800XT outperforms the 3090 by 14% in AC Valhalla at 1440p, but ends up just as fast as a 3080 in 4K. That is a somewhat surprising result that should probably raise an eyebrow? Same goes for the results in Dirt 5. Those are massive outliers that should really be talked about properly in the review.
On top of that, he includes several benchmarks where he himself states they are CPU bottlenecked (where the 3080, the 3090 and 6800XT are basically the same). It's okay to show these results and talk about them, but they're just not going to show anything worthwhile.
If you have several benchmarks that show surprising results and several benchmarks that are obviously bottlenecked by another component, then what's the point of averaging those results? That average will end up being entirely meaningless.

Last, but not least, in my experience, whenever there is something AMD is clearly behind on, Hardware Unboxed consistently tries to find reasons why that's not a big deal.
In the 6800XT review, instead of simply acknowledging that the raytracing performance of the 6800XT is not all that great and actually testing that feature properly, because it might very well become an issue in the next two to three years thanks to consoles supporting raytracing as well, the guy basically goes "meh, raytracing is too expensive anyway and it isn't worth it"... I mean, he has Metro Exodus in his benchmarks, a game that makes extensive use of raytracing. Does he include that game in the raytracing section of the review? No. He also mentions Control, probably the flagship title for that feature... also no benchmark of that title.
I don't care whether he thinks raytracing is worthwhile or not, it's the big new feature in graphics for the next few years and the big graphics feature in the new consoles, meaning it will get more use in the upcoming AAA titles. If you want to do a full review of a current high-end GPU, it has to be included and tested properly.
As for DLSS: Yes, it's not in every game... but it is in quite a few bigger games. Chances are you're going to play a few of those with your fancy new high-end GPU.
On the other hand, he claims that SAM is a huge deal and doesn't even bat an eye when he gets results in AC Valhalla that even exceed the Hitman 2 results AMD used in their marketing... and even the "worst" example of SAM in his review is among the mid range in AMD's marketing material.

Basically, IMO, the guy often fails to separate his opinion from facts and the stuff he ends up using in his reviews often feels very "confirmation biased" to me.
I'm not saying he gets paid, I'm not saying he's lying, but I do think he has a very soft spot in his heart for "the underdog" and he also really seems to like ending up with results that are "shocking".
Just go to GamersNexus and check out their review. That seems pretty comprehensive, as it always is with them. The best idea is to probably check out as many reviews as you can bear to watch / read.

text:
Looks like Big Navi is a lean and mean rasterization machine.

There are some interesting trade-offs to Big Navi to take into account. First, the Infinity Cache. Look at how much die space that takes up! That's an opportunity cost, that's space you can't put more complex ray tracing cores, or machine learning accelerators or more CUs. AMD has to squeeze that Infinity Cache for all it was worth because they sacrifice other functionality for it. Of that transistor count, how much of it is actually GPU vs. cache? Which makes it very impressive how lean the architecture is. I always wondered how fast you could make a GPU if you didn't worry about compute at all and just focused on gaming and here it is.

A second thing to consider, AMD and Nvidia have actually crossed paths again. GCN was truly a "GPGPU" design, it was competent at gaming and often bested Nvidia at many non-gaming computational loads. This was a time when Nvidia was bifurcating its designs, one for gaming, one for compute/workstation. In this latest generation, we see a flip flop, AMD has bifurcated its GPU designs into RDNA for gaming and CDNA for compute, whereas Nvidia is touting that Ampere basically good at everything, one architecture to serve all segments.

Because of this Nvidia now kind of has the perception that its design is bloated. We see that to really get the most out of Ampere, you have to be utilizing all of it, ray tracing and tensor cores included, because if you're not, that's wasted die space. Whereas the opposite is true of AMD, it's design is lean and seems fully loaded all the time, but the Infinity Cache had its trade-offs.

FINAL POINT: DLSS is not a gimmick. Simply calling it an "upscaler" undersells what is and its utility. Reconstruction of higher frequency features from a lower resolution data set is not anything new from a data processing point of view. We do it all the time with audio/video compression, we try to squeeze the highest amount of perceived "signal-to-noise" ratio from as little truth data as we can get away with. Pyschovisual encoding schemes have been the only way UHD content has made it to the masses. As resolutions continue to climb, and VRAM requirements continue to climb, GPUs and gaming engines, perhaps even entire rendering pipelines that selectively render to take advantage of this will be the future.

AMD will need a competent DLSS equivalent, if not this generation, definitely the next.
